1.text:
'Alif-Lãm-Mĩm' is the full wording of this verse, three letters at the start of Surah Al-Imran. One view leaves their meaning with Allah alone. Another sees the disconnected letters as a challenge because the Qur'an is built from letters used in ordinary Arabic speech, yet its hearers cannot bring a book like it. This reading links the opening to the form of revelation rather than assigning a certain word to each letter. A spiritual reading treats the letters as allusions about sufficiency, kindness, and harmony. A source also preserves a report about the delegation of Najran and an oath affirming Allah’s oneness. These are distinct explanations, and the verse itself does not spell out a single lexical definition. The opening also belongs to the sequence of revelation after Al-Baqarah. The prayer at the end of Al-Fatihah asked for guidance to the straight path, and the account at the beginning of Al-Baqarah presents the Qur'an as that guidance. Al-Imran begins within the same discussion of the Book, while the surah's following verses move to Allah's Oneness and the scriptures revealed before the Qur'an. The short opening therefore marks the beginning of a new surah without closing the question of what each letter means.

**What the Letters Mean.**

Alif Lām Mīm God knows best what He means by these letters. It is said that by listening to these disconnected letters [Alif Lām Mīm] which are contrary to the ordinary customs of human discourse every concept disappears from the hearts whether it be a known written cus tomary or imagined thing and whether it arises from necessity Ḍarūra sensory perception ḥiss or independent reasoning ijtihād.

**Letters in the Qur’an.**

Alif Lām Mīm – the placement of such letters has been discussed at the beginning of Sūrah Al-Baqarah. They indicate the inability of the Arabs to bring a Qur’ān like this one despite the fact that it is composed of letters similar to the ones at the beginning of this Sūrah, which also form the parts of their own speech.

**What the Letters Allude To.**

Alif Lām Mīm His saying Alif alludes to His being sufficient for you in all of your states. He is the One who sets in motion what restores you and is solely sufficient for you in what helps you. Without your asking-and even without you knowing your own state-He suffices for you even if you do not perceive it. The Lām alludes to His kindness luṬf to you at the most subtle and hidden level so much so that the locus of favor by which He strengthens you is not apparent to you. The Mīm alludes to the harmony muwāfaqa of the stream of the [divine] determination of events taqdīr with the circumstances requested by the friends.

**Guidance from Earlier Surahs.**

It will be recalled that at the end of the Surah Al-Fatihah a prayer for guidance to the straight path was made. After that, by be-ginning the Surah Al-Baqarah with 1 ‌ (This Book which has no doubt in it), it was pointed out that the prayer made in Su-rah Al-Fatihah for guidance to the straight path has been accepted and Allah Almighty has sent down this Qur'an which provides guidance to the straight path.

**Guidance and Book.**

He has sent guidance for man throughout the ages, including the Torah and the Bible, which were revealed to the former prophets. Ultimately, in accordance with God’s plan, the final book in the form of the Quran was sent down to man. The Quran is not only a genuine book of guidance but also serves as the criterion or standard of right and wrong.

**Allah and an Oath.**

And on his authority he related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: (Alif. Lam. Mim.) that he said: 'Allah informed us about the story of the delegation of Najran; it is also said that this is an oath by which Allah swore that He is One and that He has neither progeny nor partner. (Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists.)

2.text:
'Allah! There is no god worthy of worship except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining' begins with absolute oneness and states that worship belongs to Allah alone. 'the Ever-Living' rules out death and deficiency, and 'All-Sustaining' names the One who exists without dependence and sustains every created thing. The attributes explain why none besides Him deserves worship. They are not only names but the basis of the declaration. The verse gives no partner or rival a share in worship, and it presents the Creator as the One on whom the whole creation depends. The following verse speaks of the Book revealed in truth, so the statement about Allah's life and sustaining power introduces the One who sends revelation and guides. 'There is no god' excludes every object of worship other than Him, while 'except Him' makes the affirmation exclusive. The names Ever-Living and All-Sustaining provide connected grounds for that exclusivity. He does not die or diminish, and His creation remains in need of Him. All creation remains dependent on Him, while He needs nothing from creation. The attributes describe the One who is self-subsisting and sustains creation, with no death or deficiency.

**The Ever-Living and Sustainer.**

In the words (Allah: there is no god but He) which follow immediately, the doctrine of the Oneness of Allah has been put forth as a categorical declaration. (Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists) and,. (Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive) Who dies not and is not evanescent, (the Eternal) the Self-subsistent Who has no beginning. Then come the words (the Alive, the All-Sustaining) which lay out a rational proof of the Oneness of Allah. The only Being worthy of worship is the One who has always been Alive and Present and shall always live and sustain.

**Worship Belongs to Him.**

It means that there is absolutely nothing worthy of worship other than Allah. (Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists.) Therefore, it is crystal clear that all things in this world which have no power to come into being by themselves, nor can they sustain it - be they idols carved in stone, or water, or trees, or angels and apostles - none of them is worthy of worship. Allah is the One Who alone deserves to be worshipped. Bowing to the truth required them to bow to the Prophet and to God, and they thought that by surrendering to the Supreme Being and His Prophet they would diminish in stature.

**The Book That Follows.**

(It is He Who has sent down the Book to you with truth,) means, revealed the Qur'an to you, O Muhammad, in truth, meaning there is no doubt or suspicion that it is revealed from Allah. (In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)(1. Alif-Lam-Mim.)(2. Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists.)(3. It is He Who has sent down the Book to you with truth, confirming what came before it. And He sent down the Tawrah and the Injil,)(4. Aforetime, as a guidance to mankind. 'Surely nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah' leaves no place outside His knowledge. The verse names both earth and heaven and states that nothing in either is hidden. Its claim includes what people see and what they cannot see; Allah's knowledge is not bounded by human perception. It follows the account of revelation and the Standard: the One who sends guidance knows what is hidden from His servants and what they need. The next verse turns from what is hidden to Allah's shaping of people in the wombs as He wills. That sequence connects knowledge with creation; no hidden breath or unseen need is beyond Him. A servant may need what no one else perceives, but that need is not hidden from the One who creates and sustains all things. Even a breath is counted, and knowledge reaches before birth and after death, beyond what another person can observe. Allah's knowledge includes what is visible and what is hidden, and it is not limited by the senses.

**God's Knowledge of Heaven and Earth.**

Nothing no existent thing whatever is hidden in heaven and earth from God on account of His knowledge of universals and particulars. God specifies them heaven and earth because sensory perception does not go beyond these. Allah states that He has perfect knowledge in the heavens and earth and that nothing in them is hidden from His watch. He knows everything, whether it is open or hidden. Only God can truly tell us what He is in His Being and in His attributes. Not a particle exists in the heaven and earth unless He is its originator and creator mubdiʿ hi.

**Before Birth and After Death.**

And He has made this so clear in His Book, that any reader who is eager for knowledge of Him will certainly gain enlightenment from it. The right course of action for man can be determined only by a Being who has not only known man from his birth to his death, but also knows what has gone before his birth and what will happen after his death. It is, therefore, only God who, after placing the nature of man in the perspective of the entire universe, may decree what kind of conduct will guarantee man’s success in this world and the next, for a sound human mentality can only be one which is in harmony with the rest of the world and in complete accord with the vaster system of the cosmos. It is only God who has the power and the knowledge to ordain what it befits human beings to strive for in the present world. This being so, the only realistic approach for man is to trust in His Maker and accept and follow His guidance wholeheartedly and with full confidence. A servant does not breathe a single breath without God counting it muḥṣīhi.

'He is the One Who has revealed to you, O Prophet, the Book' identifies the One who sends revelation and the messenger who receives it. 'of which some verses are precise' points to clear statements whose meaning is established. 'they are the foundation of the Book' makes those verses the basis for reading the rest. 'while others are elusive' acknowledges passages whose full meaning is not immediately clear. 'Those with deviant hearts follow the elusive verses seeking to spread doubt through their false interpretations' shifts attention to the way a reader handles uncertainty: the aim is discord, not guidance. 'but none grasps their full meaning except Allah' sets a limit on what people can claim to know. Readers differ over the pause here: some stop at Allah, while others connect the well-grounded in knowledge with what follows. 'As for those well-grounded in knowledge, they say' introduces a response of humility rather than pursuit of confusion. 'We believe in this Quran' and 'it is all from our Lord' affirm the whole revelation, not only what is easy to understand. 'But none will be mindful of this except people of reason' closes by linking reflection with sound understanding. The verse does not license ignoring difficult passages; it directs interpretation back to the clear foundation and calls for faith where the full reality remains beyond human knowledge. The discussion also marks a limit: uncertainty is not permission to reject what the clear verses establish. One reading leaves the full interpretation with Allah alone; another joins those well-grounded in knowledge to the response that follows. In either case, the following words affirm that all the verses are from their Lord, and people of reason take admonition. The clear verses remain the reference point; interpretations of an elusive phrase that contradict them are rejected. Some readings call certain passages allegorical or leave their full reality to Allah, while the grounded affirm the entire Book. This restraint protects the message and the reader from turning uncertainty into discord. The following verse turns that posture into a prayer for hearts to remain firm.

The sighting of so many Muslims inspired awe in the hearts of the disbelievers, while Muslims who saw the disbelievers as twice of them turned to Allah more fervently. If the actual number of disbelievers which was three times more than their own were to be realized by Muslims, they may have been overawed. This state of sighting the numbers of the other group as twice its own was at a particular time. At another time each of the two combating groups felt the other one as low in numbers, as it would appear later in Surah al-Anfal. You saw with your very eyes, O Jews, that the unbelievers were twice the number of the Companions of Muhammad. When God wants an affair to be accomplished He makes many appear to be few in the eyes of one people and few to appear as many in the eyes of another people.

**Allah's Support and Victory.**

They had hopes of Allah's help, and ultimate victory, because they had placed their total trust in Allah, were steadfast and sincerely believed in the promise of Allah revealed to them in the following words: In spite of this, those who denied the truth suffered a crushing defeat and the believers achieved a decisive victory. This is a clear proof that God is always on the side of the believers. This serves as a demonstration from God that truth does not go unsupported. The believers actually saw the disbelievers as being double their real number; but Allah helped His allies. Allah gives His support to whomever He wishes. (And Allah supports with His victory whom He wills. Verily, in this is a lesson for those who understand.) meaning, this should be an example for those who have intelligence and sound comprehension. They should contemplate about Allah's wisdom, decisions and decree, that He gives victory to His believing servants in this life and on the Day the witnesses stand up to testify. In the face of such a great difference in resources, an extraordinary victory cannot be achieved without God’s succour.

**A Lesson for People of Insight.**

Surely in that which is mentioned is a lesson for people of vision those who are discerning so will you not be warned by this and become believers? (Lo! Herein) in Allah enabling Muhammad to triumph on the Day of Badr (verily is a lesson for those who have eyes) concerning Religion, i.e. the believers; it is also said that this means: it was a lesson for those who saw it with their own eyes. In that there is a lesson and a warning for those of insight to realize that the help of Allah can come to the believers even though they may be few in number; and that defeat can come to those on falsehood even though they may be great in number. To sum up, it can be safely said that making a small group of people with very little to fight against a much stronger group and score a victory, as prophesied in Makkah, is an unusual event full of lessons for the observant and the discerning. There are obvious signs in the words and deeds of the preacher that the Truth he preaches comes from God. If He covers the inner sight baṣīra of a people the sharpness of their physical eyes abṣār will not benefit them. (so that Allah might accomplish a matter already ordained.)[8:42] meaning, so that the truth and falsehood are distinguishable, and thus the word of faith prevails over disbelief and deviation, so that the believers prevail and the disbelievers are humiliated. They live by false explanations, until finally they leave for the next world, only to learn that the words in which they had taken refuge were utterly meaningless from the standpoint of reality.

14.text:
The verse answers a question the passage before it has left open. It opens on "The enjoyment of worldly desires, women, children" and puts the general word for appetite first, so that the particular loves that follow are read as instances of one thing rather than as separate faults. Then comes the rest of the list, "treasures of gold and silver, fine horses, cattle" and "and fertile land", the wealth that is piled up, the animals a household rides and grazes, and the fields that give a family its standing. What the next clause carries about all of it is the turning point, "has been made appealing to people", because the attraction is described as something made and given rather than as something people found for themselves, which is what makes the whole list a test and not an accident of temperament. The sentence after that measures the gift, "These are the pleasures of this worldly life", and it places the enjoyment inside one stage of a longer existence, lasting as long as that stage lasts, like the comfort of a house a traveller is going to leave. The verse then closes on the contrast the next verses take up, "but with Allah is the finest destination", the best place of return, which is not stored up here and is not lost when a person dies. Nothing in the wording condemns the things named, and the verses that follow do not condemn them either. What is exposed is the love that stops at them, and the passage goes on to put before the reader what is better. Read with the verse before it, the list does two things at once. It shows that the good things of this life are provisions rather than the goal, and it shows how easily a provision becomes the whole horizon of a life once the heart settles on it. The order of the clauses makes the point, since the destination is named last and named as the finest, and the reader is left to weigh the two.

**The love of the world and where it leads.**

The reason for this and for all evil deeds is, in fact, the love of the worldly life. It means that the love of dunya (worldly life or worldly enjoyments) is the main source of all errors. In other words, it means that all these things are there simply to serve a purpose in man's mortal life in the present world and certainly not to have him fall in love with things for their own sake, for the real beauty of the experience lies in one's ultimate resort with Allah in blissful eternity enjoying what would never perish, diminish or weaken. A world is wandering in the desert of Your love who will be given access to the Kaabah of Your acceptance? [DS 210] After He made the road of paradise that of unreached desires and disappointment, the command came, "O Gabriel:

**Why people were made to want these things.**

Why has man been made in a way that he is temperamentally attracted to these things? The first verse here names some of the most de-sired things and says that they have been made to look attractive and therefore, people go after them enticed by their glamour brushing aside any concerns for the life to come, if there be any. Allah tells us that He has made the love of desirable things of this world attractive to people in order to test them. God, wishing to ascertain which of His creatures are capable of rising above worldly attractions, has so willed it that man should be attracted to and find gratification in the things of this world, but at the same time be faced with the choice of clinging to them or renouncing them in favour of the unseen things of the next world. Allah then mentions the bounties of the life of this world that He has made attractive for the unbelievers, saying:

**The things that were made desirable.**

(Beautified for mankind is) what people's hearts find desirable is (love of the joys (that come) from women) meaning slave women and wives (and offspring) slaves and children, (and stored up heaps) amassed wealth (of gold and silver) it is also said that this means: minted or engraved gold and silver, (and horses branded (with their mark) beautiful branded horses and grazing in pastures, (and cattle) i.e. sheep, cows and camels (and land) cultivation and cultivated lands. These desirable things include women, children, wealth (in the form of gold and silver) that is overflowing and piled up, beautiful trained horses, livestock (such as camels, cows and sheep), as well as farmlands – all of which is the enjoyment of the life of the world which lasts only for a short while. Beautified for men is the love of things they covet; women, children, Qanatir Al-Muqantarah of gold and silver, branded beautiful horses (Musawwamah), cattle and fertile land. Adorned for people is love of appetites, like women, children, heaped-up heaps of gold and silver, horses of mark, cattle, and tillage. Allah mentions the delights that He put in this life for people, such as women and children, and He started with women, because the test with them is more tempting.

**How long the enjoyment lasts.**

That which is mentioned is the comfort of the life of this world enjoyed while it lasts but then perishes; but God — with Him is the more excellent abode place of return which is Paradise and for this reason one should desire none other than this abode. A believer should not become attached to these things as Allah has kept the best place of return for him: the Paradise that is as wide as the heavens and the earth. However, all these things with the external glitter of this present life will be of no use to him in the next, eternal life. (That) which is mentioned above (is comfort of the life of the world) is of benefit to people in the life of this world and then it vanishes; it is also said that this means: the joys of this world last only for as long as the stuff of any home, a bowl, a plate and the like. It is only one who makes the permanent life of the Hereafter the focus of his attention who will realize the insignificance of these worldly things.

**Paradise, and what is prepared for the servants of God.**

(But Allah has the excellent return with Him) meaning, the best destination and reward. This is the pleasure of the present world's life; but Allah has the excellent return with Him Say: (Allah! With Him is a more excellent abode) in the Hereafter, i.e. " Gabriel went and saw those adorned paradises with their infinite joy and bliss, that place of revelry made and prepared in the neighborhood of God's Presence for the exalted ones of the road and God's friends. " Then the Lord of the Worlds surrounded paradise with all the hardship and suffering of unwor thy things and unreached desires, and He made its road a bridge of trial so that everyone who aims for the Patron must first pass over that bridge of trial. Go look at it.' Go gaze on this paradise and see once what I have made and created for My servants and friends.

**How the love of these things takes hold of a life.**

If we think about it, we shall realize that it was the love for what is desirable in this mortal world which brought them out of their homes, and in this silent process, gave the world a strong and ongoing social system. A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said, "Nothing was more beloved to the Messenger of Allah than women, except horses," and in another narration, "...than horses except women." He is so engrossed in building the future of his children in this world, that he no longer remembers the fact that there is any ‘future’ beyond this present life, to which he should give thought. Making money, accumulating riches and possessing property in this world seem so estimable to him, that he fails to realize that there is any ‘wealth’ other than this, to which he should devote his life. This is not an easy choice, for he sees that worldly acquisitions lead him to an honourable place in society. This gives him the impression that it is these things that are of consequence. How should I have known which gate this is or what is the answer to the story of friendship? This is why in this case, these horses provide a shield of sufficiency for their owner, as evident by a Hadith that we will mention, Allah willing, when we explain Allah's statement,. However, as for verses where such glamorization of things has been attributed to Satan - for example, (the Satan has made their deeds look attractive to them - 8:48; 16:63; 27:24; 29:38.) - there the reference is to things that are evil, religiously and rationally; or, the reference is to a false sense of adornment which is evil because it transgresses the limits set by Allah:

15.text:
The question in this verse is asked so that it can be answered, and the answer is the rest of the verse. It opens with the command to speak, "Say, O Prophet", and then puts the question itself, "Shall I inform you of what is better than all of this", which looks back at the desires the verse before it had listed and treats them as a subject that has already been weighed. The answer comes at once, "Those mindful of Allah will have Gardens with their Lord under which rivers flow", and the condition is placed first, so that the promise belongs to a people described by their care for God rather than to everybody without distinction. The next clause carries duration, "to stay there forever", which is the exact contrast with a pleasure that lasts only as long as a stage of life lasts. The promise is then filled out with what a person longs for, "and pure spouses", and with what is greater than any of it, "along with Allah's pleasure", the contentment of God himself rather than only the gifts he gives. The verse closes on "And Allah is All-Seeing of His servants", which tells the reader that the difference between the two groups is not hidden from the one who makes the promise, and that the promise and the warning are both measured by what people do. The shape of the verse is worth noticing. It moves from a question, to a condition, to a place, to a duration, to company, and finally to God's own good pleasure, so that the list ends higher than it began, and it ends where the desires named in the verse before it cannot reach. The address to the Prophet is part of the meaning too, since he is told to put the comparison to his hearers rather than to leave them with the glitter of the world.

**Better than what was mentioned before.**

Say O Muhammad to your people ‘Shall I tell you shall I inform you of something better than that? that which has been mentioned of lusts this interrogative is meant as an affirmative. Shall I tell you about something better than those desirable things? Shall I tell you of something better than that? Here, the address is to the Holy Prophet who is being asked to tell those who become obsessed with imperfect and perishable blessings they find in the present life that he is in a position to lead them on to far better blessings. Abu Hurayrah said "The Qintar is twelve thousand Uwqiyah, each Uwqiyah is better than what is between the heavens and earth." [This was recorded by Ibn Jarir].

**The Gardens, the rivers and the purified spouses.**

For those that are fearful of idolatry with their Lord ‘inda rabbihim is the predicate the subject being the following jannātun…’ are Gardens underneath which rivers flow abiding therein decreed for them therein is eternal life when they enter it and spouses purified of menstruation and other impurities and beatitude read ridwān or rudwān meaning ‘much pleasure’ from God; and God is Seer knower of His servants requiting each of them according to his deeds. (For those who keep from evil) keep from disbelief, ascribing partners to Allah and indecencies, in reference to Abu Bakr and his fellow believers, (with their Lord, are Gardens beneath which) beneath its trees and habitations (rivers) of wine, honey, milk and water (flow, wherein they will abide for ever) they will dwell in Paradise: they shall neither die nor leave it (and pure companions) they have therein spouses who are spared menses and filth, (and contentment from Allah) and the contentment of Allah is far greater than the bliss they enjoy. Those who are mindful of Allah by fulfilling His commands and avoiding His prohibitions will have gardens with trees and palaces overlooking flowing streams in which they will live eternally. However, should there be someone there who for some unnecessary reason wishes to try farming, he will have his wish granted. According to a hadith, when the people of Paradise would have settled down there, happy and content without having any desire remaining unfulfilled, Allah Almighty will speak to them asking if they are happy and if they need anything. According to a hadith in Jami al-Tirmidhi, the Holy Prophet said: 'If a dweller of Paradise wishes to have children, the process of pregnancy, birth and growth of the child will be completed in no time and he would have what he wished for.'. They will also have wives who will be free from any defects in their form or character.

**The next life, and the permanence of what the godwary are given.**

Tomorrow, the final outcome of those whose watch word today is godwariness will be paradise and approval. The first degree is the Garden of the Shelter, and the first level of godwariness is to avoid the forbidden and the soul's caprice. After talking about the enemies, describing their life, and explaining their furthest goal, God in this verse comes back to the story of the friends. God, wishing to ascertain which of His creatures are capable of rising above worldly attractions, has so willed it that man should be attracted to and find gratification in the things of this world, but at the same time be faced with the choice of clinging to them or renouncing them in favour of the unseen things of the next world. Then Allah elucidated the bliss of the Hereafter, its permanence and favour, just as He exposited the joys of the life of this world, by saying:

**The pleasure of Allah, who is All-Seeing of His servants.**

(But the pleasure of Allah is greater)[9:72], meaning, greater than the eternal delight that He has granted them. In addition, they will gain the pleasure of Allah, and Allah will never be angry with them. 'Wordly life is cursed and cursed is what is in there, except what is used to seek the pleasure of Allah'. According to another narration: ' except the Dhikr (Remembrance) of Allah and what Allah likes and except Alim (religious scholar) and Talib ilm (student in religion).'. This Ayah means, "Say, O Muhammad, to the people, 'Should I tell you about what is better than the delights and joys of this life that will soon perish?'" Allah informed them of what is better when He said,. (And Allah is All-Seer of the servants) and, He gives each provisions according to what they deserve. (Allah is Seer of His bondmen) He is Seer of the believers, their places in Paradise, as well as their works in the life of this world. Allah sees the actions of His servants, nothing is hidden from Him and He will recompense them for what they do.

**The glitter of the present life.**

He is so engrossed in building the future of his children in this world, that he no longer remembers the fact that there is any ‘future’ beyond this present life, to which he should give thought. Providing all comforts for his home in this world becomes so dear to him that it never occurs to him that there is any other home save this, to which he should pay heed. Making money, accumulating riches and possessing property in this world seem so estimable to him, that he fails to realize that there is any ‘wealth’ other than this, to which he should devote his life. However, all these things with the external glitter of this present life will be of no use to him in the next, eternal life. This is not an easy choice, for he sees that worldly acquisitions lead him to an honourable place in society. By possessing material resources, he can have all that he wants in life. This is the pleasure of the present world's life; but Allah has the excellent return with Him Say: This is why in this case, these horses provide a shield of sufficiency for their owner, as evident by a Hadith that we will mention, Allah willing, when we explain Allah's statement,.

16.text:
This verse describes the people who are promised the Gardens in the verse before it, and it does so by putting their words on the page. It opens with the act of asking, "who pray, Our Lord", so that the mark of the group is not a claim about themselves but a habit of turning to God and addressing him. What they say begins with "We have believed", a statement about the past that they carry into the present, and the verse treats that faith as the ground of the request that follows rather than as a reward already earned. The request itself is doubled, "so forgive our sins and protect us from the torment of the Fire", and the two halves belong together, since the first asks about what is past and the second about what is to come. The order shows what they feared most, and the prayer joins a confession of faith to a plea for pardon rather than to a claim of merit. Read after the verse before it, the description is exact, because that verse had named the mindful as the people of the Gardens, and this one shows what their mindfulness sounds like when it is spoken. The whole prayer is short, and its shortness is part of its point, since the words are placed in the mouth of a whole community and can be repeated by anybody. The verses that follow turn to the deeds that accompany this faith, so the passage moves from their words to their deeds.

**Our Lord, we believe.**

Those alladhīna is either an adjectival qualification of or a substitution for the previous alladhīna who say “O Our Lord we believe in You and in Your Prophet; so forgive us our sins and guard us from the chastisement of the Fire”. (Those who say: "Our Lord! We have indeed believed") in You, Your Book and Your Messenger. (Lo! we believe) in You and in Your Messenger.

**Forgive us our sins and protect us from the Fire.**

(so forgive us our sins) because of our faith in You and in what You legislated for us. Therefore, forgive us our errors and shortcomings, with Your bounty and mercy,. (and save us from the punishment of the Fire.) (So forgive us our sins) that we committed in the pre-Islamic period as well as after the advent of Islam (and guard us from the punishment of Fire) drive away from us the punishment of hell;. O Our Lord we believe; so forgive us our sins and guard us from the chastisement of the fire that is they occupy themselves with Us entirely bi-l-kulliya and plead for help before Us at the mention of severe trials and afflictions al-raziyya.

**What the people of Paradise ask for.**

As compared to that, only three blessings of the Hereafter, that is, the gardens of Par-adise, wives purified and the approval from Allah have been identified. The people of Paradise are the ones who say in their prayers, ‘Our Lord, we have faith in You and in that which You revealed to Your messengers; and we have followed Your sacred law. According to a hadith, when the people of Paradise would have settled down there, happy and content without having any desire remaining unfulfilled, Allah Almighty will speak to them asking if they are happy and if they need anything. He will be filled with the conviction that the matters of the next world are entirely in the hands of his Lord and all the glitter of this world will appear meaningless. Whatever difficulties he faces in the path of his Creator, he will adhere to that path with total steadfastness, because he will have the conviction that no one can give him succour if he turns away from God. Apart from this, whoever has children would have them all in the Paradise. Whoever has no children in the mortal world would, to begin with, just not have the desire to have them in the Paradise. According to a hadith in Jami al-Tirmidhi, the Holy Prophet said: 'If a dweller of Paradise wishes to have children, the process of pregnancy, birth and growth of the child will be completed in no time and he would have what he wished for.'.

**The night prayer and its virtue.**

Those who spend [in good] and those who pray and beg Allah's pardon in the last hours of the night. (Every night, when the last third of it remains, our Lord, the Blessed, the Superior, descends to the lowest heaven saying, "Is there anyone to ask Me, so that I may grant him his request? Is there anyone to invoke Me, so that I may respond to his invocation? Is there anyone seeking My forgiveness, so that I may forgive him?") He will have no words to utter but—‘O my God, forgive me.’

17.text:
The previous verse put a prayer in the mouth of the believers, and this verse describes the lives that prayer comes out of, so the two read as one sentence continued. It opens with a phrase that points back at them, "It is they who are patient, sincere, obedient, and charitable", and the qualities are gathered in one line rather than separated, so that none of them is presented as the whole religion: patience in hardship, truthfulness in word and deed, obedience, and giving out of what one owns. The last words of the verse then single out one more practice, "and who pray for forgiveness before dawn", and the time is named because it costs something, since a person is asked for the prayer at an hour when sleep is sweetest. The order of the list runs from what a person endures, to what a person speaks, to what a person does with his property, and it ends in a private act of asking pardon, which keeps the whole list from becoming a display. The verse is short compared with the one before it, and its shortness keeps the description close to the single line of qualities, so that a reader can carry it. Taken with the two verses that come after it, the passage is building an argument about who has a claim on the promise, and the answer given here is not a claim but a set of habits.

**The patient, the truthful, the obedient, the giving.**

The patient in obedience and against disobedience al-sābirīna ‘the patient’ is an adjectival qualification of alladhīna ‘those’ truthful in their faith obedient compliant before God expenders of charity imploring God’s pardon by saying ‘Lord forgive us’ at daybreak’ in the last part of the night singled out here for mention because it is the time of unawareness and of the joy of sleep. (The steadfast) in performing the obligations enjoined by Allah and in shunning contraventions against Him; it is also said that this means: the steadfast when misfortunes befall them, (and the Truthful) in their faith, (and the obedient) vis-�-vis Allah and His Messenger, (those who spend) their wealth in the way of Allah, (those who pray for pardon in the watches of the night) supererogatory prayers. They are the ones who are patient in doing good actions, leaving bad actions and in the face of calamity; truthful in their words and actions; fulfil Allah’s sacred law completely; spend their wealth in Allah’s path; and ask for forgiveness in the last part of the night when prayers are most likely accepted and when hearts are not distracted. (They are) the patient, the true believers, and obedient with sincere devotion in worship to Allah. ((They are) those who are patient) while performing acts of obedience and abandoning the prohibitions. (and obedient) meaning, they submit and obey Allah,. (those who spend) from their wealth on all the acts of obedience they were commanded, being kind to kith and kin, helping the needy, and comforting the destitute. The patient, the truthful, the devoted, the expenders, those who ask forgiveness at dawn. The patient, that is, with their hearts, the truthful with their spirits, the devoted with their souls, the expenders of what they are able, those who ask forgiveness with their tongues.2 The chevaliers are those whose speaking is this and whose doing is this. These shall be the lot of those who fear Allah and are obedient to Him.

**Praying in the last hours of the night.**

(and those who pray and beg Allah's pardon in the last hours of the night) and this testifies to the virtue of seeking Allah's forgiveness in the latter part of the night. Those who spend [in good] and those who pray and beg Allah's pardon in the last hours of the night. Is it the latter part of the night yet?" and if Nafi' said, "Yes," Ibn 'Umar would start supplicating to Allah and seeking His forgiveness until dawn.

**Patient in trial, and what the qualities look like in a life.**

That is, they are patient in trial and they reject complaint until they reach the Patron, nothing of this world or the afterworld holding them back. They are patient in every trial and put aside complaint. In the heart they are patient with the Real's command, in the spirit they walk straight in the Real's covenant, in the body they observe the right ful due of the Real's command, with wealth they spend in the Real's road, with tongue they ask forgiveness and seek from the Real's generosity. They turn their faces away from both this world and the afterworld until they reach the Patron. That is, they speak the truth in seeking, so they aim straight, then they speak the truth until they witness. He will be filled with the conviction that the matters of the next world are entirely in the hands of his Lord and all the glitter of this world will appear meaningless. He will not follow his mundane desires, but will rather determine his course of action, keeping in view the court of the Almighty. There will be no discrepancy between his words and his actions. His wealth will no longer remain his, but will be devoted to the cause of God. Whatever difficulties he faces in the path of his Creator, he will adhere to that path with total steadfastness, because he will have the conviction that no one can give him succour if he turns away from God. His heart will be filled with His remembrance, and he will start calling upon Him spontaneously.

18.text:
The verse stands apart from the argument around it and states the foundation the whole sūrah rests on. It opens by naming God as a witness, "Allah Himself is a Witness that there is no god worthy of worship except Him", and the witness is his own being and his own signs rather than a statement carried from anyone else. The next clause joins two more witnesses to the first, "and so are the angels and people of knowledge", and the order is deliberate, since the angels are named as a body that carries out his command and the people of knowledge are named for what they know of his oneness, so that the reader is placed among those whose knowledge obliges them to testify to what they have found. The verse then summarises what that witness establishes, "He is the Maintainer of justice", which presents the oneness of God and the justice of his government as one subject, since a world held by one hand is a world held in order. The closing words take the testification up again in a fuller form, "There is no god worthy of worship except Him, the Almighty, All-Wise", and the repetition is there to fix the sentence rather than to add a new item to it. The two names at the end answer a possible question, since the power that no one resists is set beside the wisdom that puts everything in its place, so the reader is told both that nothing escapes him and that nothing he does is arbitrary. The verse that follows draws the conclusion, that the religion acceptable to God is the one that submits to him, and the witnesses named here are the reason the conclusion stands.

**The witness of God to Himself.**

God bears witness that is to say He has made it clear to His creation through proofs and signs that there is no god none that is truly worshipped in existence except Him He has borne witness to this and the angels have also borne witness to this by affirming it and those of knowledge from among the prophets and the believers through their conviction and in words; upholding constantly and uniquely maintaining His creations with justice qā’iman ‘upholding’ is in the accusative because it is a circumstantial qualifier and is governed by the import of the statement implied to be something like tafarrada ‘He alone is upholding…’; there is no god except Him He has repeated it for emphasis; the Mighty in His Kingdom the Wise in His actions. Allah bears witness that none has the right to be worshipped but He, and the angels, and those having knowledge (also bear witness to this); (He always) maintains His creation in justice. Allah bears witness, and verily, Allah is sufficient as a Witness, and He is the Most Truthful and Just Witness there is; His statement is the absolute truth,. (Allah bears witness that none has the right to be worshipped but He), and the angels, and those having knowledge (also bear witness to this). Allah testifies that He alone is worthy of worship based on the legislative and universal signs indicating His divinity. The Real bears witness to the Real that He is the Real. He Himself praised Himself and He Him self gave witness to Himself concerning His attributes as is worthy of Himself. He bore witness to the majesty of His measure and the perfection of His exaltedness while there was no refusal, no ignorance, no recognition by any created thing, no intellect, no conformity, no hy pocrisy, no new arrival, no heaven, no space, no shadows, no brightness. There was no universe and no Adam, no air and no space, no land and no sea, no light and no darkness, no understanding and no virtue, no conformity and no hypocrisy when the Lord of the Worlds spoke in the majesty of His measure and the perfection of His exaltedness, giving witness to His oneness and peerlessness and reporting of His attributes and Essence. There is no tawḤīd-voicer that perceives His unity, nor any attester that perceives His being.

**The angels and the people of knowledge.**

(Allah (Himself) is witness) even if no one else bears witness (that there is no God save Him. And the angels) do also bear witness to that (and the men of learning) and the prophets and the believers bear witness to that. The second testimony mentioned is that of angels who are close to Allah. They carry out His instructions and bear testimony (knowing and seeing) that Allah alone is worthy of worship. Imam al-Ghazali and Ibn Kathir find this a matter of great honour for Ulama for Allah has mentioned their witness along with His, and that of angels. The angels and people of knowledge also testify to this, by declaring and calling to His Oneness. Allah then mentioned the testimony of His angels and those who have knowledge after he mentioned His own testimony,. Then there are the Messengers and Books sent by Allah, all confirming. that truth.

**What it means that He maintains justice.**

(Maintaining His creation in justice, there is no God save Him, the Almighty) in His vengeance against those who do not believe in Him, (the Wise) and He has commanded that none shall be worshipped except Him. The God of the universe is the One and only God and He likes justice. Moreover, everything in the universe being in its right place is a proof that its Lord loves justice and righteousness rather than injustice and wrongdoing. The verse teaches the Prophet a way of addressing God about the whole question of power, and everything in it is put in the second person, so the reader is taken from the dispute about who carries authority to the one who gives it. The four clauses that follow are the heart of it, "You give authority to whoever You please and remove it from who You please" and "You honour whoever You please and disgrace who You please", and they are arranged as two pairs, the first about power and the second about standing, so that the reader is shown that both are held by the same hand. Read after the verses about the people who were deceived, the prayer is the answer to their confidence, and read with the verses after it, it is the foundation for what the passage carries next about the living and the dead. The verse also teaches the reader how to ask, since the prayer does not bargain over the outcome but places the whole of it in the hands of the one who owns it, and it asks for nothing except what the names at the end can carry. The verse takes the prayer of the one before it and fills it with the works by which the authority it names is actually seen. It opens on the turning of one thing into another, "You cause the night to pass into the day and the day into the night", and the wording describes a change that nobody can stop, since the day and the night do not argue with the hand that moves them. The next clause carries the same thought down to living things, "You bring forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living", and the pairing is put in both directions, so the reader is told that the same power that gives life also takes it away. The close then turns the whole display into a provision, "And You provide for whoever You will without limit", and the last words are what make the verse a prayer for the reader rather than a description of the sky, since a limit is exactly what he feels in his own life. Read with the verse before it, the two verses line up as a claim and its evidence, and read with what follows, it prepares for the account of the ones who were given the book and what they did with it. The order of the three clauses is also part of the meaning, since it moves from the greatest things a person can see, the night and the day, to the smallest and most personal, the food on his table, and it puts them in one sentence under one hand.

You make the night to pass to enter into the day and You make the day to pass to enter into the night each of them increasing by the amount by which the other decreases; You bring forth the living from the dead such as humans and birds from sperm-drops and eggs respectively; and You bring forth the dead the sperm-drop and the egg from the living and You provide with abundant provision whom You will without reckoning’. (Thou causest the night to pass into the day) You increase the length of the day over the length of the night, such that the day is longer than the night, (and Thou causest the day to pass into the night) You increase the length of the night over the length of the day, such that the night is longer than the day. You make the night pass into the day and You make the day to pass into the night; You bring forth the living from the dead and You bring forth the dead from the living You provide whom You will without reckoning. Mentioned after that is His unrivalled power of 'bringing the living out from the dead' such as, a chick from an egg, or a human infant from the sperm, or a tree from a seed and of 'bringing the dead out from the living' such as eggs from birds and beasts, sperm from humans or fruit from trees and dried grain from plants. A discerning reader will not fail to notice the eloquent order in which Allah's most perfect power that reigns and runs the universe from the cosmos to the soul of man has been demonstrated so effectively. The verse then states the cost in the strongest terms, "and whoever does so will have nothing to hope for from Allah", which tells the reader that the friendship in view is a matter of allegiance rather than of manners. What follows qualifies the whole thing, "unless it is a precaution against their tyranny", and the exception is about fear for one's life rather than about advantage, so a believer is not left without a way to live among people who could harm him. The verse then repeats the warning in the form of a call to caution, "And Allah warns you about Himself", and the repetition shows that the subject is grave enough to be put twice. The close gives the reason the caution is not the last word, "and to Allah is the final return", so the reader is told where the account is really kept and by whom. The verse is careful about the difference between a ruler and a friend, since the believers are not told to hate the people around them but to keep their loyalty whole, and the exception shows that same care. What is forbidden is a standing with the disbelievers against the believers, and the words for it are about allegiance rather than about daily dealing. The warning is repeated because the temptation is quiet, and it comes in the shape of an advantage rather than a crime, so the reader is handed the reason for caution in the same sentence as the caution itself. The return is named at the end because the whole rule rests on it, and the one who keeps the account is the one whose friendship is worth more than any advantage a person could take now. Read with what follows, the verse is also a fitting answer to the claims of the verses before it, since a religion that hands everything to God cannot be served by a loyalty given to his enemies.

This verse closes the story of Mary and Zachariah by naming what kind of story it is. It opens on the claim, "This is news of the unseen that We reveal to you O Prophet", and the words put the account in the category of things no bystander could have carried back, since the events happened long before the Prophet was born. The next phrase turns the claim into evidence, "You were not with them when they cast lots to decide who would be Mary's guardian", and the reader is told that the man who recites the story was not present at the meeting. The close gives the second thing he missed, "nor were you there when they argued about it", and the argument is the part that no honest report could have guessed. Read with the verses before it, the sentence explains why the whole passage could be trusted, and read with the verses after it, it introduces the second scene in the same way, so the reader is shown a method rather than a single proof. The verse also fixes the place of the story in the Qur'an's own account of itself, since the news of the unseen is given as a gift rather than as something a listener could have gathered from the people of the Book, and the reader is invited to weigh the account by its detail rather than by its fame. What the Prophet is told is not that the story is true in general but that he was absent from the moment it happened, and the two negations at the end close the door on any other source. The passage is thus teaching the reader how to read it, and every story after it is meant to be read the same way, with the same attention to what could not have been known, and the reader who takes the passage seriously is given the reason to do so here.

As stated earlier, verse 61 has instructed the Holy Prophet to invite his opponents (Christians) to Mubahalah which literally means 'mutual prayer' but in the terminology of Islamic Shari'ah it refers to a particular form of resolving religious disputes. Since curse means 'moving someone far away from the divine mercy', - and moving far away from mercy is being close to divine wrath--therefore, the essence of the meaning is: Let us think about this matter and get back to you with our decision to what we want to do.' They left the Prophet and conferred with Al-'Aqib, to whom they referred to for advice.
